name: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II)

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by defects in electron transfer flavoprotein or its dehydrogenase (ETFA, ETFB, ETFDH), impairing many flavin-dependent dehydrogenases at once
Presents as a spectrum: severe neonatal forms with or without congenital anomalies, and milder late-onset (riboflavin-responsive) disease
Severe neonatal disease features hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia and a distinctive 'sweaty feet' odour
Congenital anomalies in the severe form include large cystic (dysplastic) kidneys, facial dysmorphism and hypospadias
Late-onset MADD often manifests as a lipid-storage myopathy with exercise intolerance, muscle weakness and recurrent rhabdomyolysis
Urine organic acids show glutaric acid plus a broad range of dicarboxylic and other acids reflecting the multiple enzyme block
Acylcarnitine profile shows elevation of short-, medium- and long-chain species together, a clue to a global fatty acid oxidation defect
Many late-onset (and some ETFDH) cases respond well to riboflavin; treatment also includes fasting avoidance, glucose during crises and carnitine
reference.pathophysiology: MADD results from deficiency of electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF) or ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase (ETF dehydrogenase), which shuttle electrons from numerous mitochondrial flavin-adenine-dinucleotide-dependent dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain. Because these carriers serve the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of fatty acid beta-oxidation as well as several dehydrogenases of amino acid catabolism, a single defect simultaneously impairs oxidation of fatty acids of all chain lengths, and of glutaryl-, isovaleryl- and sarcosine-related substrates. The consequence during fasting or catabolic stress is failure of fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and energy deficiency, with accumulation of glutaric and dicarboxylic acids and secondary hyperammonaemia. ETFDH variants that destabilise the flavoprotein can be stabilised by riboflavin (the FAD precursor), which underlies the riboflavin-responsive phenotype. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated fatty acid oxidation disorders (MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD)
Isolated glutaric aciduria type I (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency)
Primary carnitine deficiency and CPT disorders
Polycystic/dysplastic kidney disease of other cause (in the neonatal form)
Inflammatory or metabolic myopathies (in late-onset disease)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing multiple chain-length elevations
Urine organic acids with glutaric and dicarboxylic aciduria
Blood gas, glucose, ketones and ammonia during crises
Creatine kinase in suspected lipid-storage myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
ETFA, ETFB and ETFDH gene sequencing
Renal ultrasound in neonates for cystic dysplastic kidneys
Trial of riboflavin with clinical/biochemical response assessment
redFlags: Neonatal hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with severe acidosis and cardiomyopathy
Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy during an acute crisis
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of renal failure
Cardiac arrhythmia or heart failure from lipid accumulation
Rapid decompensation with fasting or intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: The severe neonatal form, especially with congenital anomalies, carries a poor prognosis with high early mortality; late-onset disease is often milder and many riboflavin-responsive patients improve markedly, though relapses can occur with catabolic stress.
pitfalls: Mistaking the multiple acylcarnitine elevations for an isolated fatty acid oxidation defect
Not trialling riboflavin in a myopathic or ETFDH-related case
Allowing fasting for procedures or illness without a glucose-based emergency plan
Overlooking cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia in the acute setting
Failing to monitor for rhabdomyolysis and renal compromise in late-onset disease
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Trial of riboflavin, to which many late-onset patients respond markedly, with coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine supplementation
Dietary management avoiding fasting, with a low-fat, low-protein, high-carbohydrate diet and frequent feeds
Emergency regimen during intercurrent illness or catabolic stress using intravenous glucose to suppress catabolism and prevent decompensation
Acute management of metabolic crises by correcting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, acidosis and hyperammonaemia
Monitoring of acylcarnitine and organic acid profiles, growth, and creatine kinase where there is myopathy or rhabdomyolysis
Multidisciplinary metabolic care with a specialist dietitian
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive ETFA/ETFB/ETFDH disorder, with family screening and antenatal or newborn testing
